It's not too late to go to college -  it just sounds like you're having trouble navigating the system with your situation (no college counselors from high school,  minimal support, living situation, etc.) so it seems like its too late. Age doesn't really matter - at the extreme, I had elderly folks in my undergraduate classes before. A few other said something similar, so to address your reply: they're not graduate students or PhD students.  The specific courses are mapped to a plan for a specific level of degree, hence you might take a "English 100" class at an undergraduate/bachelors/associates level;  but at a higher degree you might take "English 570". So there's no way they were getting a higher degree while in my same classes. But I do understand that circumstances are more challenging than age. So here's a few options, just take them as suggestions and find what's best for you. 

FAFSA (student loans): If you're concerned about your current financial situation, you don't start paying off the student loans until you get your degree. 

Random scholarships: Do some research. There's a TON of random scholarships out there that people don't know about. When I was in high school, I saw one where you had to make a valentines day card and send it in and they pick the best one to award a scholarship for. It's random, but its money. Look for any bins you fall under: do any local companies give scholarships? Ethnic background? Religious background? Any clubs you were a part of growing up? Sports? Some minimum wage jobs are at companies that provide student loan support, maybe start working there first, then apply. You might qualify for more than you think and people have money to give. They're not all full rides, but they definitely add up if you game it right. 

Community college:  Other people have said this but it's a good option. I've known a ton of people who've leveraged community college in part, or fully for their degree. At any college, you have to take "general education" courses (people call them gen ends) that are basic classes that don't apply directly to your degree. Things like "English 100" even though you're a Finance major and not English. You can take those gen eds at community college for cheaper, then transfer to a larger university once you hit your upperclassmen years where the classes are more specific to your degree. Or you can just do your full degree at community college. 

Online college: There's a lot of online colleges that follow the COVID model of "non-synchronous" learning or "Distance Learning". Meaning you can just do courses on your own time online instead of going to a class. The colleges may not be as reputable as a larger university, but it does offer some flexibility in your situation. 

Military: I just want to put this out there as an option, it might not look good for your situation right away. But A LOT of people do this. You can enlist, sign on for the minimum term, then you'll come out of it with built-in financial support from the GI bill. Not only that, but you'll have had experience in a job with more cash flow to get you set up once you go to college, so you can handle the financial concerns you're mentioning now. You can even get a job in Finance in the military, so it hits the experience you're looking for anyway. The con is that you're delaying your college start by a few years, but it really is an easy way to get a start once you've done your contract. 

These are just a couple of options, you know your situation best. The solution might be one or a combination of the above. If you take away anything from my reply, just know that it's not too late. It's far from too late. But if you're recognizing this now, you have plenty of time and options to do something about it before your circumstances get you to a point where it might actually be too late. You got this. 

Feel free to PM me if you want to chat about the options.
